finding.claim: POST /settings/password sets the caller's password to the hardcoded constant 'hunter2' regardless of request input, with no re-authentication, so any caller holding a valid session can set a publicly known password on that account.
finding.source: Authenticated session for the account (stolen session cookie, or a cross-site forced request per F2). Request body is ignored.
finding.sink: set_password(g.uid, "hunter2") at routes.py:44 (set_password stub at routes.py:52-53)

trace.note: login_required aborts 401 if 'uid' not in session, else sets g.uid from session (lines 11-13)
set_password called with g.uid and literal 'hunter2'

finding.guards_checked: login_required enforces a session and binds uid to the session, not the request, so no cross-user write. No current-password check, re-auth, or MFA. Hardcoded credential violates org policy. set_password is a stub, so real impact is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: login_required (routes.py:8-16) aborts with 401 when "uid" is not in the session and binds g.uid from the session, so only a holder of a valid session can reach the handler and it can only write its own account. No current-password, re-auth, or MFA check exists in change_password (routes.py:41-45). set_password (routes.py:52-53) is a no-op stub, so real-world impact is unverified.
verdict.reason: change_password at routes.py:44 unconditionally calls set_password(g.uid, "hunter2"), and the only gate is login_required (routes.py:11-13), which requires just a valid session with no re-authentication, so anyone with a session (stolen cookie or forced cross-site request) can reset that account to a publicly known password; the trace matches the code, but the set_password stub at routes.py:52-53 means the effect is not demonstrated.

finding.claim: State-changing session-cookie routes /settings/email and /settings/password have no CSRF protection, so a cross-site page can force a logged-in victim's browser to submit them. Combined with F1 this yields account takeover.
finding.source: Attacker-hosted page auto-submitting a cross-site POST that carries the victim's session cookie.
finding.sink: change_email at routes.py:36-38 (set_email at :37) and change_password at routes.py:43-45 (set_password at :44)

trace.note: login_required only checks session presence; no CSRF token or Origin check
login_optional also performs no CSRF check

finding.guards_checked: No CSRF token, Origin/Referer check, or custom-header requirement in routes.py. Exploitability depends on app SameSite cookie config, which is not in this directory (Chrome's Lax default blocks cross-site POST cookies).

verdict.guard_found: No CSRF token, Origin/Referer check, or custom-header check exists in routes.py. The only session-related control is login_required (routes.py:11-12), which checks session presence and does nothing for CSRF. Cookie SameSite behavior is not set anywhere in this directory (no Flask config or Set-Cookie code), so the browser default applies.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: the POST routes are at routes.py:34 and :41, login_optional and login_required at :19 and :10 lack any CSRF check, and the handlers at :36-38 and :43-45 run unconditionally once reached. Whether a cross-site auto-submitted POST carries the victim's session cookie depends on SameSite settings and browser defaults that are not in this directory, and the candidate itself notes that Chrome's Lax default blocks that request, so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: POST /settings/email is reachable without a session because it uses login_optional, which never aborts, so the handler runs with g.uid=None and calls set_email(None, ...).
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, "new@example.org") at routes.py:37 (set_email stub at routes.py:48-49)

trace.note: login_optional defined; line 22 sets g.uid = session.get('uid') = None when no session; never aborts

finding.guards_checked: login_optional performs no authentication. No other check on the route. Whether set_email mishandles a None uid (NULL-row match, global update) cannot be verified because set_email is a stub.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and never aborts. The route at routes.py:34-38 has no other check. login_required (routes.py:8-16) is not applied to this route.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, routes.py:22 sets g.uid to None when there is no session, and routes.py:37 calls set_email(g.uid, ...) with no check, so an anonymous POST reaches the state-changing call with uid=None. Severity depends on the set_email stub at routes.py:48-49, which is `pass` here, so the downstream impact is unverified even though the unauthenticated write path is confirmed.

finding.claim: change_email ignores the request body and always sets the email to the hardcoded address 'new@example.org', a functional logic bug. Combined with F2 it lets a cross-site request move a victim's account email to an address the attacker does not control, causing lockout.
finding.source: Request body is never read. Trigger is any caller that reaches the route (anonymous per F3, or cross-site per F2).

trace.note: change_email handler entry; no request.get_json or request.form read
hardcoded email literal passed to set_email

finding.guards_checked: None relevant. Impact is an account-lockout or integrity issue rather than attacker-chosen takeover, so severity is low.
